At this stage itself, it may be mentioned that the
earliest of the impugned orders was passed on 28.04.2025 in B.
A. No.3308/2025 (Manohar Kumar Singh Vs. State of Jharkhand)
by the High Court. Following the said order, the orders in
respect of other accused have been passed. 
By the impugned orders, the respondents/accused have been
granted the relief of bail subject to certain terms and
conditions by setting aside the order(s) of the learned
Sessions  Judge,  who  had  declined  to  grant  bail  in  the
aforesaid cases.
We have heard learned counsel for the appellant/State and
learned counsel for the respective respondents/accused.    The
respondent/accused in SLP (Crl.) No.6599/2026 though served
has not entered his appearance before this Court.  
We have perused the impugned orders as well as the order
passed by the Sessions Court declining to grant bail in these
cases.
2

## Page 179

In order dated 12.03.2025, in the case of respondent-
accused/Manohar Kumar Singh, the Sessions Court has noted the
allegations and the details of the incident and had observed
that considering the nature of allegations and the gravity of
the offence, the Court was not inclined to enlarge the
accused/Manohar Kumar Singh on bail. It may be noted that the
deceased was none other than a police officer (Inspector of
Police).   The  allegations  were  under  Sections
103(1)/61(2)/112(2) of the  Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
and Sections 25 (1-B)a, 25(6), 26 and 27 of the Arms Act, 1959
in respect of which FIR was registered on 03.08.2024 at Kanke
Police Station.  The Sessions Court   has indicated by way of
an inference the reason as to why the relief of bail had to be
declined vis-a-vis the accused/Manohar Kumar Singh. 
 Being aggrieved, he preferred B.A. No.3308/2025 before
the High Court. The High Court in the impugned order dated
28.04.2025 has no doubt recorded the submissions made on
behalf of the respondent/accused and has only noted that the
additional public prosecutor had opposed the prayer for bail.
However, without reference to any of the material on record
nor giving any reason as to why the Sessions Court was
justified or not in declining to grant bail, the High Court
has simply proceeded to state that the accused was entitled to
the relief of bail and hence certain conditions were imposed
and bail was granted. 
Learned counsel for the appellant/State submitted that
the High Court at least ought to have stated as to why it was
3

## Page 180

not agreeing with the order passed by  the Sessions Court and
given its reasons therefore. The impugned order is  bald and
de hors any  reasoning. On that ground alone, the impugned
orders have to be set aside. He further submitted that having
regard to the several antecedents against the accused, the
gravity of offence and the nature of allegations against the
respondent/accused, the High Court ought to have engaged with
those aspects of the matter on merits and taken a decision.
That this Court may either consider the material on record and
pass an order on merits or in the alternative, if this Court
is so inclined may remand the matters to the High Court for a
fresh  consideration.  However, considering the fact that
there is a total lack of reference to the Sessions Court order
which had declined to grant the relief of bail, this Court may
direct the respondents/accused to surrender and the matter may
be considered afresh by the High Court. 
Per Contra, learned counsel for the respondents/accused,
who have appeared before this Court vehemently objected to the
submission made on behalf of the appellant/State. Firstly, it
was contended that the impugned orders were passed  in early
2025 and till date, there has been no occasion for any
grievance to be ventilated owing to or on account of there
being violation of or any breach of conditions of bail or
owing to any misconduct on the part of respondents/accused.
They have not misused their liberty. They have  cooperated
with the trial.  The trial is in progress. At this stage, it
is highly belated for the State to contend that the bail
4

## Page 181

granted to the respondents/accused has to be cancelled.
Learned counsel for the respondents also contended that
having regard to the categorical submissions made by their
counsel before the High Court, the High Court was justified in
not agreeing to or affirming the orders of the Sessions Court
declining the relief of bail and thereby has granted bail to
these respondents/accused in accordance with law.  The said
orders need not to be interfered with in these appeals as
there is no merit in these appeals. Therefore, they submitted
that the appeals may be simply dismissed. Alternatively, it
was submitted that if this Court is inclined to remand the
matters to the High Court as contended by the learned counsel
for State then, considering the  fact that they have exhibited
good conduct and behaviour, the respondents/accused may not be
directed to surrender and the High Court may be requested to
reconsider the applications for bail made by the respondents
before the High Court. 
 This argument was objected to by learned counsel for the
appellant/State by contending that having regard to the nature
and gravity of the offence and the death of a police officer,
a direction may be issued to the respondents to surrender and
the High Court may re-consider the matter.
We have noted the submissions advanced at the Bar and
perused the impugned orders of the High Court and we  have
also noted the orders of the Sessions Court and find that in
the facts and circumstances of these cases, the High Court
ought to have engaged with the order(s) of the Sessions Court
5

## Page 182

to conclude whether it was correct or incorrect on the part of
Sessions Court to decline the grant of bail, instead  the High
Court has ignored the order of the Sessions Court and without
assigning  any reasons has simply granted bail on certain
terms and conditions.
In the circumstances, we find that the ends of justice
would be met if the impugned  orders of the High Court are set
aside and the matters are remanded to the High Court  for a
fresh consideration. Since, the Sessions Court had declined to
grant bail to the respondents/accused, we find that till the
High Court decides these cases, which we have now remanded,
the  respondents/accused  shall  surrender  on  or  before
20.08.2026 before the concerned Sessions Court.  
We request the High Court to reconsider the applications
made by the respondents/accused for seeking bail.  Since, we
have directed the accused to surrender, we request the High
Court to dispose of the applications as expeditiously as
possible and in accordance with law 
The Appeals are disposed of in the aforesaid terms.
Pending application (s) shall stand disposed of. 
The orders passed in the case of the other accused simply
follow the order dated 28.04.2025 passed in B.A No.3308/2025.

2. The present appeal arises from the final judgment 
and order dated 02.09.2025 passed by the High Court of 
Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 

## Page 186

2 
 
4068 of 2024, which had partly enhanced the 
compensation awarded to the appellant for injuries 
sustained in a motor vehicle accident on 27.11.2020. 
3. The brief facts are that on 27.11.2020, the 
appellant, then aged 28 years and working as a 
labourer, met with a motor vehicle accident involving 
a Hyva Truck (Registration No. MP66D0802). The 
appellant sustained grievous injuries to both legs, 
leading to the amputation of his right leg above the 
knee and the surgical insertion of a rod in his left 
leg. The medical board certified a 90% permanent 
disability; however, the appellant contends that as an 
uneducated labourer, he has suffered 100% functional 
disability as he is now incapable of performing any 
manual labor. 
4. The proceedings originated before the IVth 
Additional Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT), 
Singrauli (M.P.) in Claim Case No. 25/2021. Vide award 
dated 24.02.2024, the Tribunal partly allowed the 
claim, awarding a total compensation of Rs. 29,59,108/- 
with 7% interest. The Tribunal assessed the appellant's 

## Page 187

3 
 
monthly income at Rs. 12,000/- based on daily wages of 
Rs. 400/-, applied a multiplier of 16 (considering his 
age as 32 years), and calculated 90% permanent 
disability.  
5. Aggrieved by the inadequate compensation and the 
lack of future prospects, the appellant preferred 
Miscellaneous Appeal No. 4068 of 2024 before the High 
Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur. The High Court, 
vide its order dated 02.09.2025, enhanced the total 
compensation to Rs. 47,09,108/ -, representing an 
increase of Rs. 17,50,000/- over the Tribunal's award.  
6. Regarding the assessment of income, we find that 
the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal and the High Court 
erroneously fixed the appellant's monthly income at Rs. 
12,000/- based on a restrictive calculation of minimum 
daily wages at Rs. 400/ -. However, a perus al of the 
record reveals that the appellant, in his deposition 
as PW -1, categorically stated he was earning Rs. 
20,000/- per month. This testimony is substantially 
corroborated by Sh. Vinay Kumar Paul, the Deputy 
General Manager of Respondent No. 1 (the employer), who 

## Page 188

4 
 
admitted in his deposition that the appellant's fixed 
salary was approximately Rs. 15,000/ - per month. 
Furthermore, the appellant provided a detailed 
breakdown of the remaining Rs. 5,000/- per month, which 
he earned through Overtime, Night Allowance, and a  
Special Allowance specifically designated for the 
hazardous nature of his work in coal mines. Considering 
these actual emoluments and the employer's own 
admissions, which were overlooked by the courts below, 
we find it just and proper to increase and fix the 
assessed monthly income at Rs. 20,000/- 
7. Upon hearing the learned counsel for both parties

O R D E R
1. Having joined the appellant institute - Post Graduate Institute of Medical
Education and Research, Chandigarh - on 29 th September, 1993 as a Welfare
Officer, the first respondent (since deceased) was subsequently promoted as an
Administrative Officer on 3rd September, 2005.  
2. Disciplinary  proceedings  were,  however,  initiated  against  the  first
respondent in 2011. It was alleged that he misconducted himself by dereliction
of duty. With full knowledge, he had signed a letter awarding a contract to M/s.
Helpline Facility Management, Noida 1 instead of M/s. Helpline Hospitality Pvt.
Ltd., New Delhi2, contrary to the approval granted by the Competent Authority.
An enquiry culminated in an order dated 13 th October, 2012 passed by the
Disciplinary  Authority,  awarding  to  the  first  respondent  the  punishment  of
compulsory retirement from service.
1  Helpline Facility
2  Helpline Hospitality

## Page 216

2
3. What  followed  is  a  series  of  litigation  wherein,  majorly,  the  first
respondent emerged successful. 
4. The first round of litigation ended with success being tasted by the first
respondent to his challenge to the penalty of compulsory retirement before the
Central Administrative Tribunal, Chandigarh 3. On a threadbare consideration of
the material on record, the Tribunal by its order dated 14 th February, 2013
allowed  the  original  application4 of  the  first  respondent.  The  order  of
compulsory  retirement  was  set  aside,  with  liberty  being  granted  to  the
Disciplinary  Authority  to  re-consider  the  matter  with  regard  to  quantum  of
punishment.
5. By  an  order  dated  29th April,  2013,  the  Disciplinary  Authority  again
punished the first respondent with an order of compulsory retirement.
6. The order dated 29 th April, 2013 was once again challenged by the first
respondent before the Tribunal by filing an original application 5. By an order
dated 12th November, 2013, the Tribunal relegated the first respondent to the
remedy of a statutory appeal. 
7. The first respondent having filed a statutory appeal on 30 th November,
2013, the Appellate Authority directed the Disciplinary Authority to obtain the
advice  of  the  Central  Vigilance  Commission6 in  writing.  The  CVC  on  10th
November,  2014  advised  the  imposition  of  a  suitable  penalty  on  the  first
respondent.  This  resulted  in  the  appellate  authority  rejecting  the  statutory
appeal  on  23rd March,  2015  with  direction  to  the  Disciplinary  Authority  to
reconsider the penalty and to pass an appropriate order.
3  Tribunal
4  O.A. No.1316/CH/2012
5  O.A. No. 587/CH/2013
6  CVC

3
8. On 7th May, 2015, the Disciplinary Authority once again passed the same
order of compulsory retirement. 
9. This triggered the third round of litigation before the Tribunal, with the
first respondent filing an original application 7 seeking quashing of the orders
dated 29th April, 2013, 23rd March, 2015 and 7th May, 2015.
10. The  original  application  again  succeeded  before  the  Tribunal.  Vide
judgment and order dated 30 th March, 2016, the Tribunal set aside the order of
compulsory retirement from service and substituted the same by an order of
withholding of two increments of pay with cumulative effect from the date the
first respondent was deemed to be reinstated in service.  The period of absence
of the respondent no.1 was directed to be treated as leave of the kind ‘due’.
Compliance was directed to be effected within a period of six weeks.
11. In terms of the order of the Tribunal, the first respondent was reinstated in
service on 11th May, 2016. 
12. Nonetheless,  while  reinstating  the  first  respondent  in  service,  the
appellant-institute challenged the judgment and order dated 30 th March, 2016
of the Tribunal before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh 8
invoking its writ jurisdiction by filing a petition9.
13. By a well-considered and well-reasoned judgment and order dated 3 rd
June,  2016  of  a  Division  Bench  of  the  High  Court,  the  writ  petition  of  the
appellant  was  dismissed.  Paragraph  20  of  the  said  judgment  records  the
detailed reasons for upholding the Tribunal’s judgment and order dated 30 th
March, 2016.

14. This appeal, by special leave was granted on 28 th November, 2016, is
directed against the High Court’s judgment and order dated 3rd June, 2016.
15. We have heard learned counsel appearing for the appellant and learned
senior counsel appearing for the first respondent, who is represented by his
legal representatives, at some length.
16. For  disposal  of  the  appeal,  we  need  not  embark  on  an  in-depth
examination  of  the  disciplinary  proceedings  initiated  against  the  first
respondent culminating in the third order of compulsory retirement. Suffice it to
note,  what  falls  for  consideration  is  whether  the  penalty  of  compulsory
retirement imposed on the first respondent was called for on facts and in the
circumstances.
17. The charge against the first respondent was:
“That  Sh.  Rajneesh  Anand,  Administrative  Officer,  PGIMER,
Chandigarh  misconduct  himself  by  dereliction  of  duties  with  full
knowledge, by way of signing the award letter given to M/s Helpline
Facility  Management,  Nodia  whereas  it  was  approved  by  the
competent  authority  to  issue  the  award  letter  to  M/s  Helpline
Hospitality, New Delhi. Sh. Rajneesh Anand by this act has exhibited
lack  of  devotion  to  his  duty  and  acted  in  a  manner  which  is
unbecoming of an employee of the Institute. In this way Sh. Rajneesh
Anand has contravened the provision of rule 3 (1) (i), (ii) and (iii) of
CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964.” 
18. It is indeed true that the first respondent committed an error in signing
the  letter  of  award  of  a  contract  to  Helpline  Facility  instead  of  Helpline
Hospitality. However, the defence raised by him before the Enquiry Officer and
the finding returned bear consideration. Defence sought to place the blame on
the shoulders of one person, who was the dealing hand. According to the first
respondent, the dealing hand obtained signature fraudulently. He signed the
final draft of award letter in good faith and confidence as the previous draft was

## Page 219

5
seen by him and found to be in order. The Enquiry Officer though found the first
respondent to have signed the “award letter” in the name of Helpline Facility,
did not return any finding that it was a deliberate act. 
19. One of the reasons assigned by the Division Bench of the High Court is
this. It was of the opinion that the Enquiry Officer having accepted the afore-
noted defence raised by the first respondent, in a way, the Enquiry Officer had
exonerated the first respondent of the charge of  dereliction of duty with full
knowledge. The charge against the first respondent not having been held by the
Enquiry Officer to be proved, the Disciplinary Authority without any note of
disagreement being intimated to the first respondent, on its own, could not
have proceeded to inflict a major penalty of compulsory retirement perceiving
the ingredient of the charge to have been established. The other reason, inter
alia, assigned by the High Court was with regard to disproportionate penalty in
the absence of any further finding as to malice, dishonesty and corrupt motive.
In the opinion of the High Court, the situation did not call for an order retiring
the first respondent compulsorily. 
20. We are entirely in agreement with the view expressed by the Division
Bench of the High Court.
21. Even otherwise, the Disciplinary Authority failed to take into account the
blemish less service career of the first respondent right from September, 1993
till  April,  2011  and  went  on  repeatedly  passing  the  order  of  compulsory
retirement evincing an intention of not retaining the first respondent in service,
come  what  may.  In  fact,  we  would  view  the  act  of  omission  of  the  first
respondent to be an aberration rather than as a misconduct warranting major
penalty. Since the penalty of compulsory retirement prematurely brings an end
to the employer-employee relationship and that severance of such relationship

## Page 220

6
is not generally favoured unless it is considered imperative to do so, the harsh
and disproportionate punishment meted out to the first respondent was not
justified  on  the  anvil  of  fairness  in  action  which  is  expected  of  employers
answering the definition of “State”. 
22. In  such  view  of  the  matter,  we  see  no  reason  to  interfere  with  the
impugned judgment and order of the High Court; hence, the appeal stands
dismissed. 
23. Service benefits like leave encashment and the benefits of the Central
Government Employees Group Insurance  Scheme have already been released.
Other benefits, i.e., gratuity and commutation of pension are yet to be released.
The same shall be released to the legal heirs/nominees as per service records,
within a period of four weeks from today.
24. Also, since provisional pension only had been released in favour of the
first respondent, pension be finalized as per rules. If the widow of the first
respondent is entitled to family pension, the same may also be released as per
rules.
25. Pending interlocutory application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CIVIL APPEAL NO. ______ OF 2026
[SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) NO.  12737-12738 OF 2026]
PADMASHREE DR. VITTHALRAO VIKHE PATIL 
SAHAKARI SAKHAR KARKHANA LTD.  Appellant (s)
                                VERSUS
THE SHRI GANESH SAHAKARI SAKHAR 
KARKHANA LTD. & ORS.  Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. These appeals arise out of the Judgment and Order
dated  19.12.2025  passed  by  the  High  Court  of
Judicature at Bombay, Bench at Aurangabad, dismissing
the  contempt  petitions  on  the  ground  that  the
petitions are not maintainable.   
3. For the present purpose, we need not dwell deep
into the facts, except to say that the maintainability
of the contempt petitions is no more res integra in
view of the Judgment and Order passed by this Court in
Alka  Chandewar  Vs.  Shamshul  Ishrar  Khan 1.   The
relevant paragraphs of the Judgment are extracted
thus:-
“48. In the face of such categorical judicial
opinion, the Delhi High Court attempted to
find  a  suitable  legislative  basis  for
enforcing the orders of the arbitral tribunal
under Section 17 in the case of Sri Krishan
v. Anand, (2009) 3 Arb LR 447 (Del) (followed
in Indiabulls Financial Services v. Jubilee
1  (2017) 16 SCC 119.

## Page 230

2
Plots,  OMP  Nos.  452-453/2009  Order  dated
18.08.2009). The Delhi High Court held that
any person failing to comply with the order
of the arbitral tribunal under section 17
would be deemed to be “making any other
default” or “guilty” of any contempt to the
arbitral tribunal during the conduct of the
proceedings” under section 27(5) of Act. The
remedy of the aggrieved party would then be
to apply to the arbitral tribunal for making
a representation to the Court to mete out
appropriate  punishment.  Once  such  a
representation is received by the Court from
the arbitral tribunal, the Court would be
competent to deal with such party in default
as if it is in contempt of an order of the
Court, i.e., either under the provisions of
the Contempt of Courts Act or under the
provisions of Order 39 Rule 2A Code of Civil
Procedure, 1908.  
49. The Commission believes that while it is
important to provide teeth to the interim
orders of the arbitral tribunal as well as to
provide for their enforcement, the judgment
of the Delhi High Court in Sri Krishan v.
Anand  is  not  a  complete  solution.  The
Commission  has,  therefore,  recommended
amendments to section 17 of the Act which
would  give  teeth  to  the  orders  of  the
Arbitral  Tribunal  and  the  same  would  be
statutorily enforceable in the same manner as
the Orders of a Court. In this respect, the
views of the Commission are consistent with
(though  do  not  go  as  far  as)  the  2006
amendments to Article 17 of the UNCITRAL
Model Law.
Pursuant to this report, sub-section(2) to
Section 17 was added by the Amendment Act
2015, so that the cumbersome procedure of an
Arbitral Tribunal having to apply every time
to the High Court for contempt of its orders
would no longer be necessary.  Such orders
would now be deemed to be orders of the Court
for all purposes and would be enforced under
the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 in the same

## Page 231

3
manner as if they were orders of the Court.
Thus we do not find Shri Rana Mukherjee's
submission to be of any substance in view of
the fact that  Section 17(2) was enacted for
the  purpose  of  providing  a  “complete
solution” to the problem.
Accordingly, we allow the appeal and set
aside the judgment of the Bombay High Court.
The matter is remanded to decide the alleged
contempt on facts. It would be open for the
respondent to argue before the High Court
that he has, on the facts of the case, not
committed any contempt”
4. We have heard Mr. N.K. Kaul, learned senior
counsel appearing for the appellant and Mr. Sudhanshu
Choudhary, learned senior counsel appearing for the
respondents at length.
5. As regards the contentions of Mr. N.K. Kaul,
learned senior counsel, that despite the clear and
categorical  order  of  injunction  by  the  Arbitral
Tribunal  dated  02.09.2024,  the  respondents  have
entered  into  mortgages,  Mr.  Sudhanshu  Choudhary,
learned senior counsel, seeks to contend that there is
no contempt because of letters dated 14.10.2024, and
30.12.2025,  wherein  the  Arbitrator-Commissioner  of
Sugar granted No Objection Certificates permitting the
Respondent 2-Bank to disburse loan amounts. We are not
inclined to examine the merits of the matters in view
of  the  fact  that  we  are  restoring  the  contempt
petitions. It is now open for the respective parties
to raise all contentions in the contempt proceedings

## Page 232

4
and the High Court will consider the same on their own
merits  and  decide  if  there  is  any  deliberate
disobedience of the order.
6. We would also request the High Court to take up
and dispose of the contempt petitions expeditiously,
preferably within three weeks from today.  
7. Pending disposal of the contempt petitions, the
interim order passed by this Court shall continue to
operate.
8. In view of above, the civil appeals are disposed
of.
9. Pending  interlocutory  application(s),  if  any,
is/are disposed of.

2. This appeal is directed against the final judgment 
and order dated 15.01.2026 passed by the High Court of 
Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh in FAO No. 4920 of 2010 

## Page 242

2 
 
(O&M). The High Court had partially enhanced the 
compensation awarded by the Motor Accident Claims 
Tribunal (MACT), Bathinda, by a lump sum of Rs. 
1,00,000/-, otherwise affirming the Tribunal's findings 
regarding the loss of dependency. 
3. The case arises from a tragic motor accident that 
occurred on 02.07.2006 at approximately 7:30 a.m. in the 
area of Village Beganwali, District Ferozepur. The 
deceased, Kanwardeep Singh, aged 39 years, was 
travelling in a Jeep (Registration No. HR -24-B-5135) 
when a Bus (Registration No. GJ-1-X-9754), driven in a 
rash and negligent manner by Respondent No. 1, struck 
the vehicle from behind. The deceased sustained fatal 
injuries and succumbed at the spot. He was an 
agriculturist and a substantial landholder, managing and 
cultivating approximately 63 acres (killas) of land. He 
was the sole breadwinner for his family, which 
originally consisted of his widow, two minor children, 
and his aged mother. 
4. The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT), 
Bathinda, vide its award dated 30.03.2010, assessed the 

## Page 243

3 
 
monthly income of the deceased at a nominal sum of Rs. 
5,000/- on the ground that since the land remained with 
the heirs, only "managerial services" were lost. 
Consequently, the Tribunal awarded a total compensation 
of Rs. 6,72,800/- along with interest at the rate of 8% 
per annum from the date of filing the claim petition 
until realization. 
5. On appeal for enhancement, the High Court of Punjab 
& Haryana, by its judgment dated 15.01.2026, affirmed 
the Tribunal’s findings regarding loss of dependency but 
granted a lump-sum enhancement of Rs. 1,00,000/-. This 
resulted in a total compensation of Rs .7,72,800/-, 
maintaining the interest rate at 8% per annum as awarded 
by the Tribunal. 
6. We find the approach of the Courts below in treating 
agricultural land as passive property to be legally 
unsustainable. The continuity of landholding in the 
hands of legal heirs cannot be treated as a substitute 
for the deceased’s earning capacity, which i ncludes 
managerial skill, supervision, and active contribution 
towards generating income. Consequently, we deem it 

## Page 244

4 
 
appropriate to increase the assessed monthly income to 
Rs. 15,000/-. 
7. In accordance with National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. 
Pranay Sethi1, an addition of 40% is made towards future 
prospects. Given the number of dependents, which 
included his widow, two minor children, and aged mother, 
a deduction of 1/4 is taken towards personal and living 
expenses.  Further, in our opinion, the claimant 
appellants are also entitled to compensation under the 
various conventional heads as per the law laid down by 
this Court in Pranay Sethi.  Therefore, we proceed to 
award Rs. 18,150/ - each towards funeral expenses and 
loss of estate, respectively, and Rs.1,93,600/- against 
the head of loss of consortium. 
8. Based on the aforementioned findings, the final 
compensation is re-calculated as follows:

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NO.  175/2017
STATE OF RAJASTHAN  & ORS.                     Appellants
                                VERSUS
         MISHRI LAL JAT                                        Respondent
O R D E R
1. This appeal by special leave, granted on 2 nd January, 2017,
is directed against the judgment and order dated 26 th August,
2016  of  a  Division  Bench  of  the  High  Court  of  Judicature  for
Rajasthan  at  Jodhpur 1 dismissing  the  appellants’  intra-court
appeal2 on the ground of delay as well as on merits.
2. The intra-court appeal was directed against the judgment
and order dated 27th January, 2015 passed by a Single Judge of the
High Court, whereby the respondent’s writ petition 3 was allowed.
The Single Judge set aside the penalty of removal imposed upon
the respondent, ordered his reinstatement in service along with
continuity in service and also directed the appellants to pay him
full  salary  with  effect  from  1 st February,  2005  together  with
interest @ 6% per annum till actual payment; for the remaining
1  High Court
2  D.B. Civil Special Appeal (W) No. 989 of 2015
3  SB Civil Writ Petition No. 4619 of 2005 
1

## Page 284

period, the respondent was granted notional benefits. 
3. Respondent was a police constable. He was tried for the
murder of head constable Ram Singh. The relevant sessions court
honourably acquitted the respondent on 1st February, 2005.
4. In the meanwhile, the respondent was proceeded against in
disciplinary proceedings. The Single Judge noted the charges as
follows: 
“(i) The petitioner after consuming liquor quarreled with Head
Constable Ram Singh, and caused him grave injuries. Thereafter,
Ram Singh was thrown down the stairs of the office of Project
Officer, Jahajpur. The petitioner did not inform anyone that Ram
Singh was lying in an injured condition at that place where he
continued  to  lie  for  whole  of  the  night  in  a  state  of
unconsciousness.
(ii) As a result of the injuries caused by the petitioner, Ram
Singh  expired  on  13.05.1996  and  an  FIR  No.  175/96  was
registered at the Police Station Jahajpur against the petitioner for
the offence under Section 302 IPC. The petitioner was arrested
and  upon the conclusion of  investigation,  a  chargesheet was
filed against him for the offence under Section 302 IPC.
(iii) In  order  to  avoid  arrest  in  the  aforesaid  case  under
Section 302 IPC, the petitioner sought and procured 10 hays
leave from the Police Line, Bhilwara on 2.5.1997. He did not join
duty on expiry of the leave period and, remained absent from
duty without permission. He returned back on 13.10.1997 and
marked his presence at the police line without any permission
for extension of leave from the higher officials. He also did not
give any explanation for the period of unauthorized absence.
(iv) Though  being  employed  in  a  disciplined  force,  the
petitioner indulged in a grave and serious offence of murder and
in  order  to  avoid  arrest,  absented  from  duty  and  thereby
committed grave misconduct.”
5. Having considered the materials on record threadbare, the
Single Judge was of the view that the facts and circumstances
giving rise to the charges in the disciplinary proceedings as well as
the evidence led in the enquiry by the witnesses were identical to
2

## Page 285

those in the criminal case and since the respondent had been
honourably  acquitted, the finding of guilt recorded against the
respondent in regard to charges 1, 2 and 4 were unsustainable in
law. In respect of charge no. 3, the Single Judge concluded as
follows: 
“……As  regards,  the  charge  No.3,  whilst  setting  aside  the
departmental authority’s findings holding the petitioner guilty of
unauthorized absence for a period of 507 days, he is held guilty
of unauthorized absence for 164 days which shall be treated as
leave without pay.”
6. As has been noted above, the intra-court appeal carried
from the judgment and order of the Single Judge failed both on
grounds of delay and on merits.
7. Before  us, learned counsel for the appellants contended
that the High Court erred in law in interfering with the finding on
charge no. 3. Since removal of the respondent from service was
not entirely based on proof of charges 1, 2 and 4 but on proof of
charge no. 3 too, the High Court ought not to have interfered with
the order of penalty. According to learned counsel, the conclusion
of the Single Judge that the actual leave of absence was for a
period of 164 days and not 507 days was also not supported by
reasons.
8. Learned counsel for the respondent is not called upon to
answer.
9. We have perused the application for condonation of delay
in filing of the intra-court appeal before the Division Bench of the
3

## Page 286

High  Court.  The  explanation  offered  was  insufficient  and,
therefore, the Division Bench was right in not condoning the delay.
10. That  apart,  we  have  examined  the  contention  touching
charge no. 3. It appears that the absence of the respondent from
service was occasioned by reason of his arrest on 17 th July, 1997.
While being in custody, the respondent could not have attended
duty.  Having  regard  to  the  same,  the  question  that  arises  is
whether the respondent should have been held guilty of absence
for  507  days.  We  have  seen  the  imputation  of  misconduct
pertaining to charge no. 3. Alleged absence was of 164 days. The
disciplinary authority could not have found any period beyond 13 th
October, 1997 as absence without authorization, since that was
not the charge. The Single Judge was right in his conclusion that
the approach of the disciplinary authority evinces no application of
mind. In any event, no exception can be taken by urging that the
judgment of the Single Judge is unreasoned. Sufficient reason has
been assigned. We have also found that the enquiry officer while
recording his conclusions did not refer to the cross examination of
the witnesses and, thereby, the report of enquiry stood vitiated.
This was brought to the notice of the disciplinary authority but to
no avail. 
11. Thus,  we  find  no  reason  to  interfere  in  exercise  of  our
appellate jurisdiction. The civil appeal is, accordingly, dismissed.
12. Connected applications, if any, stands closed.
4

appellants within a period of three months from date.

CIVIL APPEAL No. 4970 OF 2017
U.P. PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION THROUGH 
ITS CHAIRMAN & ANR. APPELLANTS
VERSUS
SUNIL KUMAR SINGH & ORS.                           RESPONDENTS
 
   
O R D E R
1. None appears for the respondents.
2. We  have  heard  Ms.  Himanshi  Girdhar,  learned  counsel  for  the
appellants.
3. Ms. Giridhar has drawn our attention to the judgment and order dated
9th December, 2016  of the  High Court of  Judicature  at Allahabad 1 under
challenge  in  this  appeal2,  whereby  a  writ  petition3 instituted  by  the
respondents came to be allowed,  inter alia .  Vide  the impugned order, the
High  Court  had  issued  the  following  directions,  summarized  for  ease  of
reference: 
1  High Court 
2  impugned order
3  Writ – A No. 28971 of 2016

## Page 296

2
a. The Uttar  Pradesh  Public  Service  Commission4 was  required  to  re-
evaluate the answer scripts of the preliminary examination of all the
candidates by deleting certain questions (i.e., questions 25, 66 and 92)
and  giving  full  marks  for  question  no.44  to  candidates  who  had
exercised option (b) or (c). 
b. The  candidates  who  were  found  to  have  qualified  the  preliminary
examination  as  a  result  of  re-evaluation  would  become  entitled  to
appear in the main examination and in respect of such candidates, the
Commission was to hold the main written examination at the earliest. 
c. The result of the main written examination which was already held, if it
had not been declared thus far, would not be declared till such time
the main written examination of the candidates who had qualified as a
result of re-evaluation were declared. In case the results of the main
written examination were already declared, no further exercise would
take  place  in  respect  of  such  candidates,  till  such  time  the  main
examination was held for the candidates who had qualified as a result
of re-evaluation.
d. The Commission was required to hold an interview from the merit list
drawn on the basis of the result of both the main written examinations
(i.e., the one held previously and the one which would be conducted
pursuant to the direction of the High Court in respect of re-evaluation). 
e. Certain candidates who appeared in the first main written examination
could fail to qualify for the preliminary examination as a result of the
High Court’s direction in respect of re-evaluation. For such candidates,
4  Commission 

## Page 297

3
their candidature would be cancelled, and they would not be entitled to
participate in the selection process further.
The High Court also took note of the statutory scheme of the Uttar Pradesh
State Public Service Commission (Regulation of Procedure) Act, 1985, as well
as  the  procedure  adopted  by  the  Commission  in  setting  the  provisional
answer  key  and  in  dealing  with  objections.  After  noting  the  statutory
scheme,  the  High  Court  observed  that  despite  the  detailed  procedure
involving  experts  at  every  step  of  recruitment,  a  large  number  of
discrepancies  had  crept  into  the  design  of  the  question  paper  and  the
answer  key.  The  High  Court  was  not  pleased  with  the  conduct  of  the
Commission, however, expressed the hope that the Commission would come
alive  to  the  responsibilities  conferred  on  it  by  the  Constitution  and
recommended  that  the  Commission  enhance  the  remuneration  of  the
experts so that the ‘mistakes’ in respect of the question paper and answer
key are not repeated in the future. 
4. According to Ms. Girdhar, the directions issued by the High Court are in
the teeth of a catena of decisions of this Court and cannot be sustained in
law. One of the decisions relied on by her in support of her contentions is
Ran Vijay Singh vs. State of Uttar Pradesh5. This Court held that:
30. The law on the subject is therefore, quite clear and we only propose to
highlight a few significant conclusions. They are:
30.1. If a statute, Rule or Regulation governing an examination permits the
re-evaluation of an answer sheet or scrutiny of an answer sheet as a matter
of right, then the authority conducting the examination may permit it;
30.2. If a statute, Rule or Regulation governing an examination does not
permit  re-evaluation  or  scrutiny  of  an  answer  sheet  (as  distinct  from
prohibiting it) then the court may permit re-evaluation or scrutiny only if it is
demonstrated very clearly, without any “inferential process of reasoning or
by a process of rationalisation” and only in rare or exceptional cases that a
material error has been committed;
30.3. The court should not at all re-evaluate or scrutinise the answer sheets
5  (2018) 2 SCC 357

## Page 298

4
of a candidate—it has no expertise in the matter and academic matters are
best left to academics;
30.4. The court should presume the correctness of the key answers and
proceed on that assumption; and
30.5. In the event of a doubt, the benefit should go to the examination
authority rather than to the candidate.
5. Having perused the impugned order, particularly in the light of the law
laid down by this Court in Ran Vijay Singh (supra) where various decisions
of the High Court are found to have been disapproved, the High Court in our
considered view exceeded the jurisdiction of a judicial review court in its
interference with the decision of experts in the academic field. The manner
of examination of  the so-called dubious  questions  pertaining  to different
topics by the High Court, as if it were an expert of experts, and in making the
directions it did are clearly indefensible.
6. We have found from the records that operation of the impugned order
was  stayed  by  this  Court  while  granting  leave  on  7th April,  2017.
Consequently, the directions were not implemented.
7. The  writ  petition  was  presented  before  the  High  Court  by  the
respondents  questioning  the  results  of  the  combined  State/Upper
Subordinate  Services  (General  Recruitment)  Examination,  2016  and
combined  State/Upper  Subordinate  Services  (Special  Recruitment)
Examination,  2016,  conducted  by  the  appellants.  Much  water  has  flown
under the bridge since then. Fresh examinations must have been held during
the last 9 (nine) years by the appellants. We, therefore, presume that the
respondents having lost interest in the matter are not represented before us.
8. Be that as it may, we set aside the impugned order. The civil appeal,
accordingly, stands allowed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).11313-11314 OF 2011
STATE OF RAJASTHAN APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
MOHD. KALEEM AND OTHERS ETC.     RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
CIVIL APPEAL NO.11404 OF 2011
O R D E R
1. Challenge in these appeals is to the common judgment
passed by the High Court of Rajasthan, Jaipur Bench,
Jaipur, dated 05.03.2010, wherein challenge made to the two
amendments in the Rajasthan Municipalities Act, 2009 (“2009
Act”),  which  have  been  made  in  terms  of  Rajasthan
Municipalities Bill, 2009, i.e., sub-sections (6) and (7)
of Section 6, which provided for 50% reservation for woman,
as also Rules 5 and 6 of the Rajasthan Municipalities
(Election) Rules, 1994 (“1994 Rules”) replacing one-third
by one-half therein, and the addition of Section 21A
between  Sections 21  and 22  of the  2009 Act  and the
consequential insertion of Rule 7A by way of amendment to
the 1994 Rules, came to be allowed.
2. The challenge to the above provisions was successful
on the ground that these amendments violated Articles 14,

## Page 319

2
243T and 243V of the Constitution of India.
3. In these appeals, service was duly effected upon the
respondent(s),  but  they  have  chosen  not  to  put  in
appearance. The reason appears to be quite obvious and
apparent. The High Court having quashed the challenged
provisions and the elections having been held and contested
as per unamended provisions and the election term stands
expired, the respondents are no more interested.
4. At the very outset, the learned Additional Advocate
General very fairly stated that the challenge to the
amendments to Section 6 of the 2009 Act and Rule 5 of the
1994 Rules have been rendered infructuous in light of the
subsequent notification issued by the State on 17.09.2009.
Consequent to the statement of the counsel for the State
the grievance qua the above provisions no longer survive.
Thus, calling for no adjudication in these appeals.
5. Learned Additional Advocate General for Rajasthan
has made an endeavour to justify the amendment which has
been sought as regards Section 21A of the 2009 Act by
asserting that the age which has been fixed and stipulated
therein, i.e., 21 to 35 years on a seat, is with an
intention to encourage youngsters. He asserts that by
providing the youth an opportunity to participate in the
election process and then become a member of the Municipal
Corporation would encourage new and fresh blood into the
system. It is asserted that this fixing of a seat for the
youth would be for a particular election only and for

## Page 320

3
subsequent election process, the seat would be fixed on the
basis of draw of lots. On this premise, he contends that
the reasoning assigned by the High Court would not be
sustainable as it has not taken into consideration this
aspect.
6. Having considered the submissions made by learned
Additional Advocate General for Rajasthan, and on going
through the impugned judgment, we are of the considered
view that the reasons as have been assigned by the High
Court while considering the provisions which were under
challenge, as has been mentioned above, i.e., Section 21A
and Rule 7A as a consequence thereof, are fully justified.
7. Fixing the age of a candidate who could participate
in the election process and that too for a specific seat,
would not fulfil the requirement as mandated under the
provisions of Article 243V of the Constitution of India.
That apart, the reasoning with regard to it being violative
of  Article  14  of  the  Constitution  would  also  be
sustainable, especially when seen in the context of the
constitutional provision as contained in Article 243V.
8. For the above reasons, we do not find any good
ground to interfere with the impugned judgment.
9. Reference, although, has been made by the learned
Additional Advocate General for Rajasthan to the judgment
in Rajbala and Others v. State of Haryana and Others 1. On
1 (2016) 2 SCC 445

## Page 321

4
perusal of which it is found that minimum educational
qualifications  were  prescribed  for  candidates  to
participate in an election for the post of Gram Panchayat,
Panchayat Samiti, or Zila Parishad in the State of Haryana.
The reasoning assigned by this Court to uphold the said
criteria i.e., minimum educational qualification was in a
different  context  and  was  not  in  violation  of  any
provisions of the Constitution of India. Whereas, in the
present case, the amendments as brought about, on challenge
have been found to be violative of Articles 14 and 243V of
the Constitution of India. The judgment as relied upon
would not be applicable to the case at hand and therefore,
not of any help.
10. Finding no merit in the present appeals, the same
stand dismissed.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. Appellant takes exception to the judgment and order dated 04 th
April, 2025 of the High Court of Himachal Pradesh at Shimla.
3. On the basis of the complaint of the respondent no.2, an FIR 1 was
registered against four accused. A-1, A-2 and A-3 (the appellant) are the
husband,  father-in-law  and  sister-in-law  of  the  respondent  no.2.,
respectively, whereas A-4 happens to a local councillor.
4. The  High  Court,  by  the  impugned  judgment,  has  quashed
proceedings against A-4, but directed the same to continue against A-1
to A-3. This essentially resulted in rejection of the appellant’s prayer for
quashing of criminal proceedings.
5. A-2 having since passed away during the process of investigation,
chargesheet was not filed against him.
1  FIR No.30/2023 dated 22nd September, 2023 under Sections 498A, 504, 506 and 34, 
Indian Penal Code
1

## Page 339

6. At the time of entertaining the special leave petition 2, out of which
this criminal appeal arises, this Court had dismissed the plea of the
husband of the respondent no.2 being the petitioner no.1 and issued
notice on the plea of the appellant.
7. We have heard Ms. Kaveeta Wadia, learned senior counsel for the
appellant, Mr. D. K. Thakur, learned counsel for the respondent no.1-
State as well as Ms. Neha Malik, learned counsel for the respondent
no.2.
8. Decisions of this Court in  Dara Lakshmi Narayana and Others
Vs. State of Telangana & Another 3 and  Digambar and Another
Vs. State of Maharashtra and Anr. 4 have been referred to by Ms.
Wadia in support of her contention that the proceedings against the
appellant ought to be quashed.
9. Ms.  Malik,  however,  contends  that  the  High  Court  was  right  in
observing, having regard to the nature of offence alleged to have been
committed by the appellant, that a mini-trial cannot be held at the stage
of considering a quashing petition and that she ought to stand trial. 
10. Having noted the contents of the FIR and the chargesheet 5 that has
since been filed, we find that the allegations levelled by the respondent
no.2 against the appellant are vague, indefinite and omnibus. Not a
2  SLP (Crl.) No.7763/2025
3  (2025) 3 SCC 735 (Paras 26, 27 and 34)
4  2024 SCC Online 3836
5  C.S. No.30/23 dated 10th October, 2023 under Sections 498A, 504, 506 and 34, Indian 
Penal Code
2

## Page 340

single  specific  incident  with  particulars  of  date  and  time,  when  the
appellant treated the respondent no.2 with cruelty, has been referred to
in the complaint. Significantly, it is admitted by the respondent no.2 that
she and the appellant, who is married since 2015, did not share the
same roof.   
11. As has rightly been submitted by Ms. Wadia, the appellant may not
have lived up to the expectations of the respondent no.2 as a dutiful
sister-in-law by attending to her during her pregnancy but that by itself
cannot and does not amount to a criminal offence for which she should
be made to stand trial.
12. Consequently,  proceedings  against  the  appellant  shall  stand
quashed.
13. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed on the aforesaid terms.
14. Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. We heard the learned counsel appearing for the parties.
2. In pursuance of our last order dated 08.05.2026, two
reports regarding the valuation of the properties  have been
placed before us . One report from Bihar, RERA and the other
report from U.P., RERA. Insofar as the valuation of the
properties bearing Nos.401 and 402, respectively undertaken by
U.P. RERA is concerned, the offer of purchase by the client(s)
3

## Page 356

SLP(Crl.)  No.4073/2025
of Mr. Parmeshwar is on the higher side. However, the client
of Mr. Parmeshwar has made a request that he would initially
make upfront payment of Rs.6 crore and for the balance amount
of Rs.16.60 crore, he wants six months time.  This, according
to us, is not feasible.  We want Mr. Parmeshwar to speak to
his client and offer the full amount within a reasonable
period of time.  In this regard, Mr. Parmeshwar prays for
sometime to take appropriate instructions.
3. Insofar as the valuation of the report forwarded by
Bihar, RERA is concerned, Mr. Vikas Singh has yet to look into
the same and respond, accordingly. 
4. There  is  one  another  property  falling  within  the
jurisdiction of UP RERA at Bachhawa, District Varanasi, Uttar
Pradesh. In this  context also although  the  UP, RERA has
undertaken the valuation, yet the client of Mr. Vikas Singh
would like to respond to the same. 
5. By the next date of hearing, we want the client of
Mr. Parmeshwar to put forward his final proposal. If he is
ready and willing to deposit th e entire amount within a
particular period of time, we may consider it accordingly, but
we are not going to allow anyone to make any payment in
piecemeal.
6. Same way, insofar as the Bihar, RERA valuation report is
4

## Page 357

SLP(Crl.)  No.4073/2025
concerned, Mr. Vikas Singh shall study the same and raise his
offer accordingly.  In other words, in tune with the valuation
report. 
7. In the course of today’s hearing, Mr. Singh also talked
about  one  plot  bearing  Arazi  No.398,  situated  at  Mauza
Kesharipur, District Varanasi, U.P. According to him, he has a
prospective buyer, who is ready to offer Rs.2 crore. However,
it has been brought to our notice that this Arazi No.398 was
already put to public auction way back in July, 2025. However,
according to Mr.Singh, the sale has not yet been confirmed.
On the next date of hearing, the learned counsel appearing for
the U.P. RERA shall place necessary details in this regard
also. 
8. Mr. Sumit Thakur, the learned counsel appearing for some
of the home-buyers has some information with regard to other
parcels of land  owned by the client of Mr. Vikas Singh.  We
want the learned counsel to place all such details by way of
an affidavit.  One copy of the affidavit shall be furnished to
the learned counsel appearing for the Bihar, RERA and one to
Mr. Vikas Singh.
9. Interim bail to continue.
10. List the matter on 17.9.2026 at 3.00 p.m.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S). 8807 OF 2026
WALCHANDNAGAR INDUSTRIES LIMITED                    …Appellant(s)
VERSUS
SWARAJ INDIA AGRO LTD.                             …Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. This appeal arises out of the order dated 11.05.2026 passed by the
National Company Law Appellate Tribunal 1 (for short, ‘the NCLAT’)
dismissing  the  interlocutory  application  for  condonation  of  delay  in
refiling the appeal and consequently dismissing the appeal, which was
filed against the judgment and order dated 29.05.2025 passed by the
National Company Law Tribunal (for short, ‘the NCLT’). 
2. The sole reason for dismissing the appeal is not for limitation in
filing the appeal, but for limitation arising due to refiling. The judgment
of the NCLT was delivered on 29.05.2025 whereas the appeal was
filed  on  28.06.2025.  Ms.  Madhvi  Devan,  learned  senior  counsel
appearing for the appellant submits that the delay has not occurred as
a solitary instance. She has brought to our notice, five instances where
1 In I.A. No. 991 of 2026 in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 291 of 2026.
1

## Page 379

the Registry had notified the defects i.e., on 21.07.2025, 01.08.2025,
29.11.2025, 22.12.2025 and also on 29.01.2026.  As against each of
these notifications by the Registry, the appellant submits that attempts
were  made  to  cure  the  defects  on  28.07.2025,  25.11.2025,
08.12.2025, 28.01.2026 and finally on 02.02.2026. In view of the fact
that defects were not notified at one breath, but were spread over five
distinct dates, we are of the opinion that the process undertaken in
rectifying the defects can be dealt with liberally. This will however be
subject to payment of costs. As regards the reliance placed by learned
counsel  for  the  respondent  upon  the  judgment  in  the  case  of  CA
Ramchandra  Dallaram  Choudhary  vs.  Adani  Infrastructure  and
Developers Private Limited 2, we find that it will not apply in the facts
and circumstances of the case. The view taken by us is in the facts
and circumstances of the case, particularly when the defects were
notified multiple times and also cured successively, particularly when
the  last  defect  notified  on  29.01.2026  was  rectified  and  refiled  on
02.02.2026 itself. 
3. In view of the above, we allow the Civil Appeal No. 8807 of 2026,
set aside the order passed by the NCLAT in  I.A. No. 991 of 2026 in
Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 291 of 2026 dated 11.05.2026 and restore
the Company Appeal to its original number subject to the appellant
2 2026 SCC Online SC 1097,
2

## Page 380

paying Rs. 2,00,000/- (Rupees Two lakhs) to the respondent as costs. 
4. With these directions, the appeal stands allowed.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay  in  filing  and  refiling  the  petition  @ Diary  No(s).29138/2024  is
allowed. 
2. Having  heard  the  learned  Advocate  General  appearing  for  the
petitioner(s)  and  the  learned  advocates  appearing  for  the  respondents,  we
notice  that by advertisement dated 28.08.2021, applications  from intending
eligible  candidates for recruitment against existing vacancies of Contractual
Trained Graduate Teacher (Arts), Trained Graduate Teacher (Science - PCM),
and Telugu Teacher posts in Government Secondary Schools of Odisha came to
be issued. Under Clause 5(a), it was clearly indicated that the candidates must
have attained the age of 21 years and must not be above the age of 32 years as
on  01.01.2021.  Questioning  the  said  Clause  5(a),  Writ  Petition  (Civil)
No.29806/2021 and connected matters came to be filed seeking for upper age
relaxation of at least two years by modifying Clause 5(a) of the advertisement.
3. It was contended that the last date of application was in 2019, and due to
then prevalent COVID pandemic, the recruitment did not take place. By an
2

## Page 384

interim order dated 28.09.2021, the High Court granted submission of offline
copy  before  the  last  date.  Accordingly,  the  offline  applications  of  the
respondents were accepted, and they were allowed to appear in computer-
based test for the post applied but results were not declared. In the meanwhile,
with effect from 11.01.2022, the Odisha Civil Service (Fixation of Upper Age
Limit) Rules, 1989 came to be amended whereunder the upper age limit was
enhanced to 38 years and made applicable to the advertisements issued during
the calendar years of 2021, 2022, and 2023.  A proviso came to be inserted on
15.01.2022 which is to the following effect:
“No.  1424-GAD-SC-RULES-0008-2016/Gen-  In  exercise  of  the
powers conferred by the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution of India,
the Governor of Odisha is pleased to make the following rules further to
amend the Odisha Civil Service (Fixation of Upper Age Limit) Rules, 1989,
namely:-
1. Short title and commencement:- (1) These rules may be called the
Odisha  Civil  Service  (Fixation  of Upper Age  Limit) Second  Amendment
Rules, 2022.
(2) In the Odisha Civil Service (Fixation of Upper Age Limit) Rules, 1989,
after the second proviso to rule 2, the following proviso shall be inserted,
namely:
“Provided also that upper age limit as so fixed in the second
proviso shall be applicable to those cases where the last date of
application for recruitment to any post as per the advertisement
issued is still not over as on the date of commencement of the
Odisha Civil Service (Fixation of Upper Age Limit) Amendment Rules,
2022.”
4. A similar writ petition came to be filed by Alekha Kumar Sethy, where the
High Court declined to interfere  with the advertisement and the prayer for
enhancement of upper age limit. The said order has been confirmed by this
Court in SLP (Civil) Diary No.9259 of 2023 vide order dated 05.04.2023.
5. The  High  Court  in  the  instant  case  had  allowed  the  writ  petition  on
18.04.2023 and directed the State to publish the results of the candidates. An
intra-court appeal filed with an application for condonation of delay did not yield
3

## Page 385

any result, and the impugned order came to be passed dismissing the writ
appeal.
6. In view of the State itself having taken a decision to enhance the age by
amendment of the Rules, in the facts obtained in the present case, we do not
propose to interfere with the impugned order. However, we make it clear that
subject to the writ petitioners  being qualified, or in other words, not being
disqualified as per the rules, the State shall proceed to process their claim in
accordance with the extant rules, keeping in mind the order of the learned
Single  Judge  as  affirmed  by  the  Division  Bench.  With  this  observation,  the
present Special Leave Petitions stand disposed of. However, we make it clear
that it is confined to the present writ petitioners / writ applicants only and it
shall not be treated as a precedent.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. 
  (NEHA GUPTA)                                   (AVGV RAMU)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 10072/2016
EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR (PERSONNEL) LIFE 
INSURANCE CORPORATION OF INDIA, 
CHENNAI APPELLANT 
VERSUS
  P. JAYAPRAKASH AND ANR.       RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. We  have  heard  Mr.  Gautam Narayan, learned  senior  counsel
appearing for the appellant and Mr. Jayanth Muth Raj, learned senior
counsel appearing for the first respondent.
2. We need not refer to the multiple rounds of litigation which have
preceded the present appeal under consideration by us.
3. Suffice it to note, a writ petition 1 is pending on the file of the
High Court where the first respondent has challenged the determination
made by the Committee in its decision dated 03 rd January, 2020 that
the first respondent does not belong to a Scheduled Tribe and such
petition is due to be heard by the High Court shortly.
4. Insofar as the impugned judgment and order is concerned, the
1  WP.3350/2020

## Page 403

same  directs  the  appellant  to  treat  the  respondent  as  a  general
candidate and to retain him in service.
5. Such a direction, however, is unsustainable, having regard to the
fact  that  not  only  was  the  respondent’s  claim  of  belonging  to  a
Scheduled Tribe not accepted earlier by the Scrutiny Committee but the
same has also not been accepted in the decision under challenge in the
writ petition referred to above.
6. We are of the considered opinion that interest of justice would
be best served, if the following order is made. We, therefore, order  that
:
(a) The impugned judgment and order is set aside.
(b) Since the first respondent has only a year’s service left if
he were to continue in service, the High Court is requested to
decide WP.3350/2020 in accordance with law, as expeditiously as
possible.
(c) All contentions and points on merits are left open to be
urged before the High Court by the parties and decided by it.
(d) Should  the  High  Court  be  of  the  opinion  that  the  first
respondent’s claim of belonging to a Scheduled Tribe is genuine
and that the Committee arrived at an erroneous finding, it shall be
open to the High Court to make appropriate orders on the first
respondent’s claim, including a direction for his reinstatement in
2

## Page 404

service but upon hearing the appellant.
(e) In such an event, the respondent shall be entitled to all
benefits pertaining to the post.
(f)On the contrary, if the claim of the respondent is found to be not
genuine and unacceptable, and the Committee's finding is upheld,
the first respondent shall not be entitled to any further benefit
arising out of his service till 2004.
7. The civil appeal is disposed of on the above terms.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand closed.
…………………………….J.
(DIPANKAR DATTA)
………….………………….J.
(SHEEL NAGU)
NEW DELHI; 
AUGUST 04, 2026.

1. Leave granted.
2. The  High  Court  of Gujarat at Ahmedabad, by the  impugned
judgment and order dated 8 th May, 2026, has rejected the appellant’s
application for bail.
3. Appellant was arrested on 17 th February, 2026 in connection
with FIR/I.C.R. No.11210008260081 of 2026 dated 13th February, 2026
registered  at Police  Station  Sarthana,  District-Surat,  Gujarat  under
Sections 386, 420, 504, 506(2) and 114 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 and Sections 25(1-B)(A) and 27(1) of the Arms Act, 1959.
4. We have heard learned counsel appearing for the parties and
perused the materials on record.
5. The FIR named the appellant and two others as accused. The
latter have been granted protection by the High Court and such order

## Page 411

2
has not been challenged. 
6. Allegation in the FIR is that loan amount has not been repaid,
despite assurance. 
7. T aking an overall view of the matter in the light of the nature of
allegations and the period of incarceration, we are of the considered
opinion that the appellant need not be detained in custody any longer
and that he could be admitted to an order for release on bail pending
trial.
8. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned judgment and order.
9. Appellant shall be released on bail, subject to furnishing of bail
bonds to the satisfaction of the trial court and subject to such other
terms and conditions as may be imposed by it.
10. Needless  to  observe,  the  appellant  shall  not,  directly  or
indirectly, by making inducement, threat or promise, dissuade any
person acquainted with the facts of the case from disclosing such
facts to the court.
11. In the event there is any breach of the terms and conditions for
grant of bail, the trial court shall be at liberty to cancel the bail of the
appellant.
12. It  is  also  ordered  that  the  appellant  shall  diligently  attend
proceedings  of  the  trial,  unless  exempted.  If  he  abstains  from
attending the proceedings without justifiable cause, that could also be
seen as breach of the conditions for grant of bail and the trial court

Criminal Appeal No.1526 of 2022
     Heard Mr. Ranjan Mukherjee, learned Counsel for the
appellants and Mr. Nishant Awana, learned Advocate-on-
Record for the respondent-State of West Bengal.
2. The present Interlocutory Application No.40054 of
2026, which is restricted to only appellant no.1-Dilu
Ghosh, is for suspension of sentence and grant of bail to
him during the pendency of appeal before this Court.
3. Learned  counsel  for  the  appellants  submits  that
though the appellant no.1-Dilu Ghosh had been convicted
under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860 and sentenced to life imprisonment along with a
fine of Rs.5,000/- (Rupees Five Thousand) but the only role
attributed was that he was present at the site when the
incident occurred. It was submitted that during trial also,
nobody has testified that the appellant no.1-Dilu Ghosh had

## Page 420

3
any overt role to play.
4. Learned counsel for the appellants drew the attention
of  the  Court  to  an  order  dated  25.01.2023,  where  a
Coordinate Bench of this Court while hearing the prayer for
bail to the appellants of the present case, had granted
bail to the appellant no.4-Badan @ Swarup Ghosh/co-accused
basically on the ground that he had been imprisoned for
close to nine years. It was submitted that in the said
order dated 25.01.2023, with regard to the appellant no.1-
Dilu Ghosh, it was observed that if the appeal is not heard
within a reasonable period, he may renew his prayer for
bail. Learned counsel further submitted that the appellant
no.1-Dilu Ghosh is in custody for almost nine years now.
5. It was submitted that even otherwise, for the purpose
of assisting the Court, it would be relevant that the
deceased had a chequered history with a number of criminal
antecedents.
6. Learned Advocate-on-Record for the respondent-State
of West Bengal submits that the Trial Court had found the
appellant no.1 guilty.
7. Having considered the facts and circumstances of the
case and taking into account the period of incarceration
and the relief given to the appellant no.4/co-accused, we

## Page 421

4
are inclined to allow the prayer for suspension of sentence
and grant of bail to the appellant no.1-Dilu Ghosh.
8. Accordingly, the sentence of the appellant no.1-Dilu
Ghosh is suspended and he is directed to be released on
bail, subject to such terms and conditions as may be
imposed  by  the  Trial  Court.  Interlocutory  Application
No.40054 of 2026 stands disposed of.
9. As the original records of the Courts below have been
received and the soft copies of the same have been provided
to the learned counsels for the parties, let the matters be
placed for hearing on 20.11.2026.

O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Leave granted.
3. We have heard Mr. Anil Kaushik, learned Additional Solicitor
General of India on behalf of the appellant as well as Mr. Neeraj
Kumar Singh, learned counsel for respondent No.1 – M/s. Marion
Biotech Private Limited and Mr. Dinesh Kumar Goswami, learned
senior counsel for respondent Nos.2 to 6.
4. In our considered opinion, the appellate authority under the
Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 had, on both occasions, namely,
while passing the order dated 11.08.2023 whereby the appeal of the
first respondent was allowed in part, as well as while passing
review order dated 04.10.2023, failed to apply its mind to the
relevant material on record and to supply cogent reasons in support
of the conclusions reached.
1

## Page 423

5. Consequently, both the aforementioned orders are set aside and
the appeal filed by respondent No.1 against cancellation of its
licence by the Drug Controller is restored to its original number
and file. We direct the appellate authority to hear and decide the
appeal(s) afresh.
6. It is, however, clarified that we have not expressed any
opinion on merits of the case. It goes without saying that until
the appeal(s) is decided, the order of the Drug Controller shall
continue  to  operate.  As  a  necessary  corollary,  the  impugned
judgment of the High Court dated 19.05.2025 is also set aside.
7. The appeals stand disposed of, accordingly.

“……. 
8.  This  Court  has  heard  the  learned  counsel  for  the

of this Court has been complied, doesn’t find any reason
to proceed further in the contempt matter. However, it is
made clear that the petitioner(s) is/are at liberty to file
appropriate application/petition if he/they has/have still
any grievance with regard to any entitlement(s), which
has not been endowed upon him/them. …….”
2. In view of clause 10 of the Letters Patent of the  High Court, and as
explained by this Court in Midnapore Peoples’ Coop. Bank Ltd. & Ors. Vs.
Chunilal Nanda & Ors. 3, the remedy of an intra-court appeal is available to
the petitioners before the relevant Division Bench of the High Court.
3. Since such remedy has not been pursued and no exceptional case has
been set up for entertaining a special leave petition without the remedy of an
intra-court appeal being pursued, we are not inclined to entertain this special
leave petition; hence, the same stands disposed of without any interference
with the impugned order.
4. We grant liberty to the petitioners to pursue their remedy, either before
the Division Bench of the High Court or in terms of the liberty granted by the
Single Judge in the impugned order before an appropriate forum.
5. It  is  abundantly  made  clear  that  we  have  not  examined  the  rival
contentions on merits and all points are left open to be urged by the parties
before the appropriate court. 
6. Should an intra-court appeal be presented before the Division Bench of
the  High Court within 30 (thirty)  days, the  Division Bench may proceed to
decide the appeal on its own merits without limitation creating a bar.  Having
regard to the lapse of time since initiation of the original proceedings, it would

IN

SANTOSH & OTHERS                                  PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF HARYANA & OTHERS                         RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Delay in filing the Review Petition is condoned
2. The application seeking oral hearing is rejected. 
3. The  present  Review  Petition  arises  from  the  judgment  and  order  dated
28.01.2026 passed by this Court in SLP (C) No. 4058 of 2026, whereby the Special
Leave Petition filed against the judgment dated 14.10.2025 passed by the High Court
of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh, in RSA No. 786 of 1998 was dismissed. 
4. It has been averred in the Review Petition that a fundamental error apparent on
the face of the record has occurred inasmuch as the entire proceedings relating to the
assessment of compensation and allotment were undertaken without the issuance of
the  mandatory  statutory  notice  in  Form  VII  under  Section  16(2)  of  the  Haryana
Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1972. 
5. We have carefully gone through the material placed on record. It appears that
both the First Appellate Court and the High Court considered the substantial questions

## Page 465

2
of law raised before them and by reasoned judgments, decided the same against the
petitioners. This Court also, after analysing the entire material on record, dismissed
the Special Leave Petition filed by the petitioners. Therefore, the judgment sought to
be reviewed does not warrant any interference by this Court.
6. A review is not an opportunity to re-argue the merits of the case or to seek a
rehearing merely because the appellate courts have reached a conclusion different
from that of the trial Court. Hence, no ground much less any valid ground for review
has been made out by the petitioners.
7. Accordingly, the present Review Petition is dismissed. 
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

Sentence  Application  (Appeal)  No.1675/2025  in
D.B.Criminal Appeal No.316/2025 whereby the High Court
dismissed the suspension of sentence application of the
petitioner.  The  petitioner  has  been  convicted  under
Section 302 read with 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
and sentenced to undergo life imprisonment and a fine of
Rs.5,000/-  (Rupees  five  thousand)  with  default
stipulation.
3. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  petitioner
submits that the petitioner is 91 years of age and he has
already undergone 10 months imprisonment. 
4. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State
vehemently opposes the prayer for suspension of sentence.
5. Having  considered  the  overall  facts  and
circumstances and, especially the age of the petitioner,
we are inclined to suspend the sentence of the petitioner
and enlarge him on bail, pending hearing of the Criminal
Appeal No.316 of 2025 on the file of the High Court of
Judicature for Rajasthan, Bench at Jaipur.

1. Heard  Mr. Nachiketa Joshi, learned Senior Counsel for
the petitioners and  Mr. Vinay Sharma, learned counsel for the
respondents.

## Page 552

2
2. The present petition calls in question the correctness of
the order dated 30-06-2026 in CWP No. 10322/2026 passed by the
High Court of Himachal Pradesh at Shimla whereby the High
Court  stayed  the  notification  dated  24.06.2026  and  the
subsequent modification and also allowed the petitioners along
with similarly situated persons, to continue till further
orders.
3. When the matter came up for hearing on 03.08.2026, the
following order was passed:-
“1. Application for exemption from filing certified
copy of the impugned judgment is allowed.
2. Learned senior counsel drawing attention to the
prayer clause in the Writ Petition submits that the
individual respondents who were the writ petitioners
before the High Court herein had not even challenged
the validity of the Himachal Pradesh Panchayati Raj
(Amendment) Act, 2025 and, more particularly, Section
20 of the amending Act which in turn amended Section
120 of the principal Act and inserted sub-Section (4).
After the amendment, Section 120(4) reads as under:
“(4) If a Panchayat is not constituted due to
forcemajeure conditions or boycott by general
public or due to some other reasons after the
issue  of  election  programme  by  the  State
Election Commission, the term of such Panchayat
constituted later on shall run concurrently
with other Panchayats of the State.” 
3. Learned senior counsel submits that two of the writ
petitioners had even lost the election. Learned senior
counsel submits that till date, the petitioners are in-
charge and the whole purpose of the amendment was to
bring uniformity in the conduct of elections and the

## Page 553

3
tenure  of  Panchayats  constituted  pursuant  to  the
elections. Learned senior counsel submits that the
amendment enables the State to hold elections in one
go.
4. Learned senior counsel further contends that the
High Court by staying the operation of the Notification
dated 24th June, 2026 has rendered Section 120(4), as
amended, nugatory and otiose.
5. Issue notice, returnable on 10th August, 2026.
6. Liberty is granted to serve dasti, in addition.
7. Till the next date of hearing, there shall be
interim stay of operation of the impugned order.
4. The main matter is coming before the High Court on
12.08.2026.
5. We are of the opinion that till the matter is heard and
decided by the High Court, the arrangement as was made by the
order of this Court, dated 03.08.2026 extracted hereinabove,
should continue.
6. Accordingly, the impugned order shall remain stayed till
the High Court finally decides the main matter. 
7. With the above observations, the Special Leave Petition
is disposed of.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

the High Court of Andhra Pradesh at Amaravati 1 suspends payment of cheque
amount with the following directions: 
“i. The  petitioner  herein  is  directed  to  surrender
before the learned Judicial Magistrate of First Class, at
Vizianagaram, within one week from this day and, on
such surrender, the petitioner shall be enlarged on
bail  on  executing  a  personal  bond  for  a  sum  of
Rs.20,000/- (Rupees T wenty Thousand only) with two
sureties for a like sum each to the satisfaction of the
learned  Judicial  Magistrate  of  First  Class,  at
Vizianagaram, on the same day.
ii. The petitioner shall deposit the fine amount of
Rs.5,00,000/-  which  is  imposed  before  the  learned
Judicial  Magistrate  of  First  Class,  at  Vizianagaram,
within  a  period  of  one  (1)  week  from  this  day.  In
default of deposit of amount, as ordered  supra, the
interim  suspension  granted  today,  shall  stand
cancelled automatically without further reference to
the Court.
iii. The petitioner shall appear before this Court as
and when directed pending disposal of the revision.”
6. By an interim order dated 02 nd July, 2026 passed by a Co-ordinate Bench
of this Court while issuing notice on this special leave petition, it was inter alia
directed as follows: 
“……. 8. Subject to deposit of Rs.2,50,000/- (Rupees
T wo Lakhs Fifty Thousand only) before the Registry of
this  Court  within  a  period  of  four  weeks,  by  the
petitioner, the operation and effect of the impugned
order dated 02.03.2026 passed by the High Court of
Andhra Pradesh at Amaravati in IA No. 2/2026 in Crl.
R.C.  No.216  of  2026,  particularly  insofar  as  the
direction  requiring  deposit  of  Rs.5,00,000/-,  shall
remain stayed.”

directing  modification  of  clause  (ii)  (supra)  of  the  impugned  judgment  by

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. IA No. 115834/2021 for condonation of delay in
filing, is allowed.
2. It is common ground that in W.P. (PIL) No. 116
of 2018, the High Court of Uttarakhand has observed
that the action of the State Government in not
regularizing  the  employees  sponsored  through  the
agency of UPNL and to deny them minimum of pay scale
including  Dearness  Allowance  is  arbitrary  and
unreasonable.
3. The High Court thereafter issued the following
directions in paragraph 34 of the judgment:
2

## Page 580

“34. Accordingly,  the  writ  petition  is
disposed of with the following directions: 
A. The State Government is directed to
regularize  the  employees  sponsored
through UPNL in a phased manner within
a  period  of  one  year  as  per
regularization schemes framed from time
to time.
B. The State Government is directed to
ensure that the employees sponsored by
UPNL  get  minimum  of  pay-scale  with
dearness allowance along with arrears
to be paid within a period of six
months from today. 
C. The respondents are directed not to
deduct any GST or Service Tax from the
salary of the employees sponsored by
UPNL.”
4. The above order passed by the High Court was
challenged  before  this  Court  in  Civil  Appeal
Nos.7181-7317 of 2021 and the same has been affirmed
vide order dated 15.10.2024.
5. In view of the above, the Writ Petition(s) /
Special Leave Petition(s) are disposed of with the
observation that the present batch of petitioner(s)
shall also be entitled to the benefit of directions
issued by the High Court in W.P. (PIL) No. 116 of
2018.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

IA No. 215913/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING C/C OF I/JUDGMENT, IA
No. 215914/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.
 
Date : 07-08-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE K.V. VISWANATHAN
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE ARUN PALLI
For Petitioner(s)  Mr. Mohit D. Ram, AOR
    Mr. Rajul Shrivastav, Adv.
                   Ms. Nayan Gupta, Adv.
                   Mr. Tejas Rai, Adv.                   
For Respondent(s) 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard  Mr.  Mohit  D.Ram,  learned  counsel  for  the
petitioner(s).
2. The High Court obviously made an inadvertent error in
recording that the limitation provided under Section 34 of the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (for short, ‘A&C Act’)
was 120 plus 30 days. However, that makes no difference for the
reason that in the present matter the award was pronounced on
18.09.2024. The 90 days period, prescribed under the Statute as
part of the limitation, expired on 17.12.2024. The respondents
had a further period of 30 days before which they could file

## Page 775

2
application under Section 34 of A&C Act. That further 30 days
period, in terms of Section 34(3) of A&C Act,  would have
expired on 16.01.2025. However, on 06.01.2025, it is not
disputed that the application under Section 34 of A&C Act was
filed and soon thereafter, the office objections were removed,
and application under Section 34 of A&C Act numbered on
31.01.2025.
3. Under the circumstances, if we ignore the error of the
High Court and compute limitation afresh, the application under
Section 34 of A&C Act has been filed within the extended period
of 30 days.
4. For the reasons stated above, we find no good ground to
interfere with the impugned judgment/order(s).
5. The Special Leave Petition is dismissed in the above
terms.
6 Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
(NIRMALA NEGI)                                  (MANOJ KUMAR)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        COURT MASTER (NSH)

petitioner regarding the firing of a weapon.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the first respondent has,
at the outset, fairly offered to pay the subject amount of Rs. 44
lakhs to the petitioner within two weeks. The said offer is
acceptable to the learned counsel appearing for the petitioner. The
issue  regarding  the  deposit  of  the  said  amount  and  the
consequential entitlement of the other family members of the
petitioner is  sub judice  before National Company Law Tribunal,
Indore Bench (in short, ‘NCLT’). 
2. We  direct  the  NCLT  to  decide  the  said  controversy
expeditiously and preferably within three months. Needless to
observe that all the contentions of the parties are left open to be
raised before the NCLT.
3. In  view  of  the  subsequent  developments,  the  directions
contained in our order dated 01.08.2025, directing the Reserve Bank
of India to conduct a financial audit of the accounts of the first
respondent, have becomes infructuous. The said directions are,
accordingly, recalled.
4. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of in the above terms
with a direction that the parties shall abide by the statements
made before this Court.
5. All  pending  applications,  including  application  for
intervention/impleadment, stand disposed of.

under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.
2. Upon filing of such Writ Petition, the High Court will
consider the issue uninfluenced by the earlier observations.
3. With this clarification, the Writ Petition stands dismissed as
withdrawn. 
(KAPIL TANDON)                                  (NIDHI WASON)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             ASSISTANT  REGISTRAR
